props.title: Brewster McCloud
props.initialSlug: Quirky tale of a boy who dreams of flying in Houston

sections.content: Brewster McCloud stands as Robert Altman's most bizarre and audacious follow-up to his breakthrough hit **M*A*S*H** (1970). This surreal dark comedy follows a young man living secretly in the Houston Astrodome while building mechanical wings to achieve human flight. Altman crafts a wickedly subversive satire that blends elements of murder mystery, coming-of-age story, and mythological allegory. The film's structure mirrors a twisted lecture on bird behavior, complete with an ornithologist narrator who gradually transforms into a bird himself. This experimental approach showcases Altman's early mastery of overlapping dialogue and ensemble staging that would become his signature in classics like Nashville (1975) and The Long Goodbye (1973).

sections.content: The film's cynical view of authority and institutions reflects the counterculture movement of the early 1970s. Bud Cort's innocent yet determined Brewster represents youth rebellion against societal constraints, while Sally Kellerman's mysterious Louise symbolizes both protection and destruction. Altman populates his frame with eccentric characters and running gags, including Michael Murphy's hot-shot detective wearing different disguises in every scene. The director's trademark zoom shots and roving camera work transform the Astrodome into a character itself - a massive artificial cage that both shelters and imprisons Brewster's dreams of flight.

The film's influence can be seen in later works that blend magical realism with social commentary, like Being There (1979) and The Fisher King (1991). Its DNA is particularly evident in Wes Anderson's films, especially Rushmore (1998), which shares its Houston setting and theme of youthful obsession. The bird imagery and commentary on human nature anticipates later works like Birdman (2014) and Black Swan (2010), where the desire to transcend human limitations leads to both triumph and tragedy. sections.content: Brewster McCloud represents the peak of Altman's early experimental phase, alongside films like That Cold Day in the Park (1969) and Images (1972). The director would continue pushing boundaries throughout his career, but never again with such unbridled surrealism. The film's circus-like finale in the Astrodome, complete with a literal ring announcer and death by bird droppings, remains one of cinema's most audacious endings.
